units.title: Why Was Science Born?
units.sub: Modern science didn’t appear out of nowhere. It grew in a soil that believed “the world is orderly and can be understood.”

share.v: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter.

blocks.h: Have you ever wondered why scientists believe that a law measured in the lab today will still hold tomorrow? Why do they believe that physics on earth also applies to the most distant stars?

This isn’t something experiments can prove; it’s something you have to believe before you can run an experiment at all. Modern science grew rapidly in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe, and many of the people studying nature then believed the world had been made by a wise Creator.
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter.
Three things you must believe first

items: Nature is orderly: the world is not a battlefield of moody gods; it runs according to fixed laws.
Humans can understand it: made in God’s image, the human mind can grasp the patterns of creation.
It is worth studying: creation is good, not an illusion or something lowly, so it is worth hands-on observation and experiment.

blocks.h: Science is like a jigsaw puzzle. You’re willing to spend hours on it because you believe the pieces in the box all belong to the same picture. If the pieces had been cut at random, nobody would bother trying.

In 1925 the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued in Science and the Modern World that Europeans’ confidence that science is possible came from medieval theology’s insistence on the rationality of God. His conclusion: “faith in the possibility of science … is an unconscious derivative from medieval theology.”

In 1938 the sociologist Robert Merton pointed out a close link between the values of seventeenth-century English Puritans and the Royal Society members’ commitment to experimental science, an idea later called the “Merton thesis.”

The Australian historian Peter Harrison has taken this further. After the Reformation, readers of the Bible paid more and more attention to its literal and historical sense, and no longer treated the things of nature mainly as allegorical symbols but as things worth studying directly. In addition, many seventeenth-century scholars believed that the Fall had damaged human senses and reason, so careful, repeated experiments were needed to correct ourselves. Both ideas shaped the rise of experimental science.

Harrison also cautions that the modern categories “science” and “religion” were not sharply divided in the seventeenth century as they are today. Looking back through today’s framework can easily oversimplify history.
Many founders of modern science, such as Kepler, Boyle and Newton, openly said that their research was connected with their faith in the Creator.

Whitehead, Merton, Harrison and others argue that the Christian doctrine of creation was one important cultural soil for the rise of modern science. Scholars accept that this influence existed, but its extent is still debated.

The strong claim that “without Christianity there would be no science” lacks sufficient evidence. The rise of science also involved Greek philosophy, the scholarly heritage of the Islamic world, printing, the university system, economic conditions and many other factors.

The best explanation for why the universe is orderly and also intelligible to the human mind is that it comes from a rational Creator. This is a philosophical inference, not an experimental conclusion.
His wisdom: hiding mysteries for us to seek
God did not write every answer across the sky. He hid mysteries within creation and invites us to explore. Exploring is itself an honor.
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter.
The prophet Jeremiah uses “the ordinances of heaven and earth” as a picture of the reliability of God’s covenant. The steadiness of the laws of nature is itself a shadow of God’s faithfulness.
Yahweh says: “If my covenant of day and night fails, if I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth,
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
Today, when you switch on a light or check the weather forecast, pause and think: all of this rests on the fact that “the world has laws.”
Reflect: Do I take the order of the world for granted, or do I see a faithful God within it?

Prayer: Lord, Creator of heaven and earth, thank You for giving the world its fixed laws and for giving us minds that can understand them. Help me to see Your wisdom in my studies and my work, and to give the glory to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Change your mindset and you change your life: science began with an idea, that the world can be understood. My mindset also sets the direction of my life.
From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: studying nature is not competing with faith; it is looking into the glory God has hidden.
The Bible is my standard: when we see science through the Bible’s view of creation, we need neither fear learning nor worship it.

blocks.h: This week: Pick one pattern that happens every day (the time of sunrise, the shape of the moon, a plant’s growth) and record it for seven days in a row, each day offering God one sentence of thanks for His faithfulness.
Quiz

quiz.q: Early modern scientists believed that “today’s laws will still hold tomorrow.” Where did this confidence come from?
o: It was fully proven by experiments
It is a conviction needed before experimenting, linked to believing the world is orderly
quiz.e: The stability of natural laws is a precondition of science, and many early scientists connected it with the Creator’s faithfulness.

quiz.q: Which statement about “Christianity and the rise of science” is the most careful?
o: Science would have been impossible without Christianity
The two have nothing to do with each other
The Christian view of creation was one important soil, alongside many other factors
quiz.e: Scholars acknowledge the influence, but its extent is still debated and should not be exaggerated.

quiz.q: According to Proverbs 25:2, to conceal a thing is whose glory?
quiz.e: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter.”

units.title: Kepler: Following the Creator’s Thoughts
units.sub: He meant to become a pastor, but ended up praising God in the orbits of the planets.

share.v: The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.

blocks.h: For two thousand years, people believed the planets must move in perfect circles. The German astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) spent years calculating the position of Mars and found it off by just a tiny amount: only 8 arcminutes.
He didn’t hide that small discrepancy. He faced it honestly, and in the end overturned the thousand-year tradition of circular orbits: planets move in ellipses.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.
Kepler’s three laws

items: First law: planets orbit the sun in ellipses, with the sun at one focus.
Second law: the line joining a planet and the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves faster near the sun and slower far from it.
Third law: the square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.

blocks.h: The second law is like a figure skater spinning: arms pulled in, she spins faster; arms stretched out, she slows down. A planet speeds up near the sun and slows down farther away, yet always obeys the same rule.

The first two laws were published in 1609 in the New Astronomy, and the third in 1619 in The Harmony of the World. These laws later became an important foundation for Newton’s theory of universal gravitation.

At the University of Tübingen, Kepler had been preparing to become a Lutheran pastor. In 1595 he wrote to his teacher Michael Maestlin: “I wanted to become a theologian; for a long time I was restless. Now, however, behold how through my effort God is being celebrated in astronomy.”

In 1599 he wrote to Herwart von Hohenburg about the laws of nature: “Those laws are within the grasp of the human mind; God wanted us to recognize them by creating us after his own image so that we could share in his own thoughts.”

The widely quoted line “thinking God’s thoughts after Him” has never been traced to Kepler’s own writings. It should be treated as a later summary, not quoted as his actual words. The letter to Herwart above is the closest in meaning.
Kepler’s first and second laws were published in 1609 in the New Astronomy, and the third in 1619 in The Harmony of the World.

Kepler was trained in theology at the University of Tübingen and remained a devout Lutheran all his life; from 1612, because he did not accept some teachings of the Formula of Concord, the pastor in Linz barred him from Communion.

Kepler’s astronomy was deeply shaped by his theology; for example, he compared the sun, the sphere of fixed stars and the space between them to the Triune God. Scholars differ on how far this influence went.
The saying “thinking God’s thoughts after Him” is often attributed to Kepler, but no original source has been found; it is a traditional attribution.
That the universe can be described by elegant mathematics, and that the human mind happens to understand that mathematics, points to a rational Creator. This is a philosophical inference.
His wisdom and faithfulness: the stars keep their appointed courses
What Kepler saw was a God of order. For ages upon ages the planets have followed the same laws, just as God’s Word says:

Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. By the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, not one is lacking.

Yet Kepler’s life was far from easy: his wife and children died young, war drove him from place to place, and his mother was accused of witchcraft, and he personally defended her. In his suffering he still looked up to the order of the heavens.
When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?
Tonight, take a moment to look up at the sky. Find a planet or the brightest star, and think about how it is moving along the orbit God has set.
Reflect: When the facts don’t match what I originally thought, am I willing to face them honestly like Kepler, or will I keep only the answers I like?

Prayer: Heavenly Father, the heavens declare Your glory. Thank You for letting us understand the laws You have set. Make me honest and humble, willing to be corrected by the truth, both in my learning and in my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Review and correction: Kepler rethought everything over an error of 8 arcminutes. In the eight steps of changing our mindset, review and correction are keys to growth.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: Kepler was not a pastor by profession, yet in astronomy he brought praise to God. My work can too.
The Holy Spirit is my guide: keep looking up even in hard times, and ask the Holy Spirit to guide me along God’s orbit.

blocks.h: This week: Identify one opinion you have long held onto that may need correcting. Bring it to God in prayer, and share it honestly with one of your spiritual companions.
Quiz

quiz.q: What shape did Kepler discover planetary orbits to be?
quiz.e: This overturned the two-thousand-year tradition that planets move in perfect circles.

quiz.q: What is the most accurate thing to say about the line “I am merely thinking God’s thoughts after Him”?
o: It comes from chapter 1 of Kepler’s New Astronomy
It is often attributed to Kepler, but no original source has been found
quiz.e: The closest in meaning is his 1599 letter to Herwart.

quiz.q: According to Psalm 19:1, what do the heavens declare?
quiz.e: “The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.”

units.title: The Truth About the Galileo Affair
units.sub: It wasn’t as simple as “science versus religion,” and the Church wasn’t blameless either.

share.v: You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.

blocks.h: Many people have heard the story: because Galileo said the earth goes around the sun, the Church threw him in prison and tortured him, and as he left he muttered, “And yet it moves.”

The real history is more complicated than that story, and more worth pondering. Galileo really was subjected to an unjust trial, but he was not imprisoned, and there is no evidence that he was tortured; the famous line first appears in writing more than a hundred years later.
He who pleads his cause first seems right; until another comes and questions him.
What happened

items: 1610: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) uses a telescope to see the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, supporting Copernicus’s heliocentric model.
1616: the Roman Congregation of the Index declares heliocentrism contrary to Scripture, and Galileo is warned not to hold or defend it.
1632: he publishes the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, putting Pope Urban VIII’s arguments in the mouth of a character named “Simplicio.”

1633: the Inquisition finds him “vehemently suspected of heresy” and requires him to publicly abjure heliocentrism; his sentence of imprisonment is immediately commuted to house arrest, and he spends the rest of his life at Arcetri near Florence, dying in 1642.

blocks.h: It’s like a family quarrel that gets retold as a story of “good guys versus bad guys.” The truth involves power, saving face and academic factions, as well as genuine scientific questions. Reduce it to a slogan, and you miss the real lessons.

Galileo himself was a Catholic and did not oppose the Bible. In his 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, he quoted Cardinal Baronius: “the intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven and not how heaven goes.”

In Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion (2009), edited by the historian of science Ronald Numbers, Maurice Finocchiaro shows that Galileo’s forced recantation and house arrest are facts, but “prison” and “torture” are later exaggerations. During his interrogation he was threatened with torture, but there is no evidence it was actually used.

Heliocentrism also still faced real scientific problems at the time: for example, stellar parallax could not be observed (it was not measured until 1838). And Galileo’s argument from the tides to prove that the earth moves later turned out to be wrong. All of this means the affair was not simply a matter of clear right and wrong.
In 1633 Galileo was found “vehemently suspected of heresy,” forced to abjure heliocentrism, and kept under house arrest for life; he was not put in prison.
“And yet it moves” (Eppur si muove) first appears in a 1757 work by Baretti; neither the trial records of the time nor his student’s biography mention it, and it is generally regarded as legend.

Besides theology and science, the Galileo affair also involved the breakdown of his relationship with the Pope and academic and political power struggles. Historians still debate how much weight each factor carried.
In 1992, in an address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, Pope John Paul II acknowledged on behalf of the Roman Catholic Church that the theologians of that time had misunderstood Scripture.
Scripture and nature both come from the same God; real conflict exists only in people’s mistaken interpretations of the two. This is a theological and philosophical inference.
His righteousness: truth is not afraid to be examined
This history teaches us two lessons. First, don’t attack others with simplified stories. Second, when the church does wrong, admit it honestly instead of making excuses for it.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.
God is righteous. He does not need anyone to protect His name by unrighteous means. When God’s people use power to crush others, it is God’s own name that is harmed.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
Be still for a moment and think of a time you jumped to a conclusion after hearing only one side.
Reflect: When I, or a group I belong to, get something wrong, do I rush to defend it, or am I willing to admit it before God?

Prayer: Righteous God, forgive me for the times I have put pride and power in the place of truth. Make me love the truth and speak honestly, and make Your church humble and teachable. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: there was pride on both sides of the affair. Humility means returning to our proper place, letting God be God, and not crushing people with power.
People matter more than issues: when we argue about ideas, we must not hurt people. The other person is someone God loves, not an enemy to defeat.
Let Jesus reign: the point is not that I win, but that the truth prevails.

blocks.h: This week: The next time you hear a story about how “such-and-such group is terrible,” check what the other side says before deciding whether to pass it on.
Quiz
