o: He was thrown into a dungeon for years
He was forced to abjure heliocentrism and kept under house arrest for life
quiz.e: His sentence of imprisonment was immediately commuted to house arrest.

quiz.q: What is the more reliable view of the line “And yet it moves”?
o: It is clearly recorded in the trial records
Galileo wrote it at the end of the Dialogue
It first appears in a source from 1757 and is generally regarded as legend
quiz.e: None of the records from the time mention it.

quiz.q: Galileo quoted the saying that “the intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven and not how heaven goes.” Who originally said it?
quiz.e: He quoted it in his 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina.

units.title: Newton: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy
units.sub: The same law governs the falling apple and the moon in its course.

share.v: He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.

blocks.h: An apple falls to the ground, yet the moon doesn’t fall down. Isaac Newton’s (1643–1727) insight was that the force that brings the apple down and the force that holds the moon are actually one and the same.

In 1687 he published the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, using a single body of mathematics to explain falling bodies on earth, planets in the sky and the tides in the sea. For the first time, heaven and earth were united under one set of laws.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
The law of universal gravitation

items: Three laws of motion: inertia; force equals mass times acceleration; action and reaction.
Universal gravitation: any two bodies attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Uniting heaven and earth: Kepler’s three laws of planetary motion can be derived from these laws.

blocks.h: The moon is actually “falling” toward the earth all the time; it is also moving sideways fast enough that it never falls down, so it keeps circling the earth. It’s like swinging a ball on a string: the pull of the string is gravity.

In 1713 the second edition of the Principia added the General Scholium, in which Newton wrote: “This most elegant system of the sun, planets, and comets could not have arisen without the design and dominion of an intelligent and powerful being.” He also said this Being “rules all things, not as the world soul but as the lord of all.”
In 1692 he wrote to Richard Bentley, who was giving the Boyle Lectures, that when he wrote the book he had hoped its principles would help thoughtful people believe in a God.
Facing it honestly: Newton’s unorthodox theology

Newton left a huge body of manuscripts on theology, biblical prophecy and church history. Historians studying them have found that he privately rejected the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, regarding it as a later corruption of the church, and believed some Bible passages supporting the Trinity had been altered by later hands. He concealed these views in public.

We can admire Newton’s reverence for God and his insight into nature, while stating clearly that on the core doctrine of the deity of Christ, he departed from the faith of the church through the ages. A great scientist is not a theological authority.
Newton published the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy in 1687, setting out the laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation.
The General Scholium first appeared in the 1713 second edition of the Principia and speaks explicitly of God’s wisdom and dominion.
According to his private manuscripts, Newton did not accept the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity; there is broad consensus on this among Newton scholars.

The story that “Newton thought of gravity when an apple fell” comes from his own recollections to friends late in life; the details may have been embellished later, but it is not a complete fabrication.

That the laws of nature are stable, universal and describable by mathematics fits with the Bible’s statement that “in him all things are held together.” This is a theological and philosophical inference.
His faithfulness: all things are held together in Him
Newton saw the laws; the Bible tells us about the One behind the laws. The universe is not a self-sustaining machine; it is upheld moment by moment by God’s word.

His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself made purification for our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;

This verse says that the One who upholds all things is the very Son who made purification for our sins. Newton saw the greatness of the laws; all the more should we know who the Lord is who gave them.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made.
…Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
Pick up something small and let it fall. This simple motion obeys the laws that govern the entire universe.
Reflect: Do I treat brilliance as a guarantee of faith? Is the Jesus I believe in the One revealed in the Bible?

Prayer: Lord Jesus, all things are held together in You; You are the Word, and You are God. Guard my heart, so that I am not puffed up by knowledge, but stand firm in the truth and worship You in love. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: Newton’s greatness deserves admiration, but the example for my life is Jesus, not any celebrity.
The Bible is my standard: whatever authority is speaking, go back to the Bible and test it.
Humility overcomes pride: knowledge puffs up; the more we understand, the more humbly we should worship.

blocks.h: This week: Read John chapter 1, write down three statements about who Jesus is, and share them with a friend.
Quiz

quiz.q: According to Newton’s law of universal gravitation, how does gravity relate to distance?
o: It is proportional to the distance
It is inversely proportional to the square of the distance
It does not depend on distance
quiz.e: Double the distance, and the pull becomes a quarter of what it was.

quiz.q: In which edition of the Principia did Newton’s General Scholium first appear?
o: It was published only after Newton’s death
quiz.e: The General Scholium was added in the second edition and speaks of God’s wisdom and dominion.

quiz.q: Which statement about Newton’s faith is more accurate?
o: He was a model of orthodox Trinitarian theology
He did not believe in God at all
He revered God, but privately rejected the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity
quiz.e: Scholars see this clearly in his manuscripts.

units.title: Pascal and Boyle
units.sub: One met God on a night of fire; one wrote his faith into his will. Two experimenters, one shared devotion.

share.v: You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.

blocks.h: After the French mathematician Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) died, a servant found a small piece of parchment sewn into the lining of his coat. For years, whenever he changed clothes, he had unpicked it and sewn it into the new garment.

It read: “The year of grace 1654, Monday, 23 November … from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight. Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars.” It came to be called the “Memorial,” and that night the “Night of Fire.”
You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.
Pascal: from air pressure to the Pensées

items: Calculator: as a teenager, he designed a mechanical calculator to help his father with tax calculations.
Air pressure experiment: in 1648 he had his brother-in-law Périer measure the height of a mercury column at the top and bottom of the Puy de Dôme, showing that air pressure decreases with altitude.
Pascal’s principle: pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted evenly throughout; this is the principle of today’s hydraulic press.
Probability: in 1654 his correspondence with Fermat laid the foundations of probability theory.

blocks.h: Reason is like a flashlight: it can light up many things. But to truly know a person, a flashlight isn’t enough; you also need trust and an open heart. Knowing God is the same.

The Pensées contain the famous line: “The heart has its reasons of which reason knows nothing.” Pascal was not opposing reason; he was saying that we come to know truth not by reasoning alone, but also with the heart.
Pascal planned to write a book defending Christianity but died before finishing it. His notes were gathered and published in 1670 as the Pensées, which include his famous “wager” argument.
Boyle: experiment and devotion

In England, Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was one of the founding members of the Royal Society. In 1662 he published the inverse relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas, today’s Boyle’s law. His emphasis on experiment, public records and repeatable verification shaped the practice of modern science.

Boyle was also a devout Anglican. He funded the printing of the Bible in Irish and wrote works such as The Christian Virtuoso (1690). In 1680 he was elected President of the Royal Society but declined because of scruples of conscience about taking oaths. In his will he endowed lectures to defend the Christian faith: the “Boyle Lectures,” first given by Richard Bentley in 1692 and revived in London in 2004.
Pascal’s “Memorial” records his experience on the night of 23 November 1654 and was found after his death in the lining of his clothing.
The 1648 Puy de Dôme experiment was carried out by Périer and showed that air pressure decreases with altitude.
Boyle’s law was published in 1662; the Boyle Lectures were established under his will and began in 1692.

The relationship in Boyle’s law was first proposed as a hypothesis by Henry Power and Richard Towneley; Boyle established it by experiment and published it. The attribution of the name is debated among historians.
Pascal’s wager is not meant to prove that God exists, but to challenge people about the choice they face in view of eternity; it is a philosophical and apologetic argument.
His faithfulness: the covenant-keeping God meets people personally
Pascal was a first-rate mathematician, but what he met on the Night of Fire was not an abstract “First Cause”; it was the God who made a covenant with Abraham and keeps it.
Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
Science lets us see God’s works; but knowing God Himself requires that He reveal Himself, and that our hearts be open to Him.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches.
Pascal sewed the night he met God into his coat and carried it with him. What is the sign of your encounter with God?
Reflect: Is the God I know a concept from a book, or a God I have personally met and walk with every day?
Prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, I don’t just want to know about You; I want to know You. Kindle my heart with Your fire, and help me seek You with all my heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit: Pascal said the heart has reasons that reason does not know. Don’t just use your head and rely on yourself; use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry: both scientists’ work flowed out of their living relationship with God.
Multiplication: Boyle invested his resources in Bible translation and lectures so that the faith would be passed on. I can also invest in the faith of the next generation.

blocks.h: This week: Write down one experience of truly meeting God, keep it somewhere you always carry (your phone or wallet), and find a chance this week to share it with someone.
Quiz

quiz.q: Where was Pascal’s “Memorial” found?
o: Sewn into the lining of his clothing
quiz.e: He carried it with him for years, sewing it into his new clothes each time he changed.

quiz.q: What does Boyle’s law describe?
o: The relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas
quiz.e: At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume.

quiz.q: Which God did Pascal write about on the Night of Fire?
o: The God of the philosophers and scholars
A distant God who doesn’t get involved
The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
quiz.e: “Not of the philosophers and scholars.”

units.title: Faraday and Maxwell
units.sub: A bookbinder’s apprentice who never went to university, and a mathematical genius: together they unlocked the secret of light.

share.v: Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.

blocks.h: The phone in your hand, the lights at home, the generators at the power station: behind them all is one discovery, that a changing magnetic field can produce an electric current. In 1831 the Englishman Michael Faraday (1791–1867) discovered electromagnetic induction.
In that same year, James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) was born in Scotland. Some thirty years later, he used a handful of equations to unite electricity, magnetism and light.
Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.
From induction to light

items: Faraday: a blacksmith’s son who served as a bookbinder’s apprentice and had almost no formal education; he taught himself by attending Sir Humphry Davy’s lectures and went on to become the master experimenter of the Royal Institution.
Electromagnetic induction: move a magnet inside a coil of wire, and the coil produces a current; this is the principle of generators and transformers.
Lines of force and fields: Faraday pictured the space around a magnet filled with invisible “lines of force,” an idea that later developed into the “field” of physics.

Maxwell: he put Faraday’s pictures into mathematics, publishing his theory of the electromagnetic field in 1865 and predicting that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light: light is an electromagnetic wave.

blocks.h: Faraday was like a painter, drawing the lines of force with his eyes and hands; Maxwell was like a composer, setting that picture to a symphony of mathematics. One relied on experiment, the other on mathematics, and only together did they see the whole picture.

After Maxwell’s death, his theory was confirmed when Heinrich Hertz, in the late 1880s, produced and detected electromagnetic waves experimentally. Today’s radio, radar and Wi-Fi are all built on this foundation.

Faraday belonged to a very small denomination, the Sandemanians. He made a public profession of faith in 1821, later served twice as an elder, and often visited poor and sick members. He declined a knighthood and twice declined the presidency of the Royal Society. In an 1854 lecture he said, in substance (paraphrased here), that God’s works in nature can never contradict the higher things that belong to our future life.

In 1871 Maxwell became the first Cavendish Professor of Experimental Physics at Cambridge and oversaw the building of the Cavendish Laboratory. Over the laboratory’s great door, Psalm 111:2 was carved in Latin: “Magna opera Domini exquisita in omnes voluntates eius.” It is generally believed that Maxwell chose the verse; when the new laboratory opened in 1973, the same verse was also carved in English at the entrance.

Maxwell was wholeheartedly involved in church life all his life. In a letter to his wife he wrote, in words to this effect (paraphrased here), that the more we enter together into the work of Christ, the more room He has to do His work in us.
Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831; Maxwell published his theory of the electromagnetic field in 1865, showing that light is an electromagnetic wave.
Faraday was a member of the Sandemanian church and served twice as an elder.
Psalm 111:2 is carved in Latin over the door of the old Cavendish Laboratory.
That Maxwell chose this verse for the inscription is stated in most sources, but direct documentary evidence from the time is scarce, so it is best to say “it is generally believed.”
That electricity, magnetism and light in nature can be united by a few elegant equations reflects a faithful and wise Creator. This is a philosophical inference.
His faithfulness: the source of light
Maxwell discovered that light is an electromagnetic wave, but the Bible tells us the source of light:
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
Physical light lets us see the world; Jesus, the true Light, lets us see the path of life.
Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
Turn on a lamp and watch the light fill the room. Light travels about 300,000 kilometers every second, yet it obeys a few simple equations.
Reflect: Do I delight in God’s works? Am I willing to take time to “ponder” His work in my life?

Prayer: Father of lights, thank You for saying “Let there be light,” and for sending Jesus to be the light of the world. Shine into the darkness of my heart, help me follow You, and make me a light to others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: Let Jesus reign: Faraday declined a knighthood and chose to be plain “Mr. Faraday.” When we let Jesus reign, we don’t need to chase human glory.

235 spiritual companions: Faraday and Maxwell, one with experiment and one with mathematics, completed each other. I also need spiritual companions (the 235 pattern of walking together) who complement me.
Build God’s kingdom system: carving a psalm over the laboratory door declared God’s sovereignty in the workplace.

blocks.h: This week: Put a Bible verse (for example, Psalm 111:2) on your desk, at your workplace or as your phone wallpaper, and read it every day before you start work.
Quiz

quiz.q: What did Faraday discover in 1831?
quiz.e: A changing magnetic field can produce an electric current in a coil.

quiz.q: According to Maxwell’s electromagnetic theory, what is light?
quiz.e: He calculated that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light.

quiz.q: Which verse is carved over the door of the Cavendish Laboratory?
quiz.e: “Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.”

units.title: Mendel: Genetics in the Monastery
units.sub: In a monastery’s small vegetable garden, a friar grew peas and discovered the laws of heredity.

share.v: So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.

blocks.h: Why do children take after Dad in some ways and Mom in others, and why do some traits “skip a generation” before reappearing? Before the nineteenth century, people generally assumed that parents’ traits blended together like paint.
In the Abbey of St Thomas in Brno, in today’s Czech Republic, an Augustinian friar named Gregor Mendel (1822–1884) spent years growing and counting tens of thousands of peas, and found the answer.
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
What the peas taught us

items: Choosing the right material: peas are easy to grow, their pollination can be controlled, and they have clear contrasting traits, such as round or wrinkled, yellow or green seeds.
Seven pairs of traits: Mendel tracked flower color, seed shape, seed color, pod shape, pod color, flower position and plant height.

Three to one: crossing pure-bred round and wrinkled peas gave a first generation that was all round; when the first generation self-pollinated, the second generation was round and wrinkled in a ratio of about 3 to 1.
Hereditary factors: he reasoned that heredity is determined by paired “factors” that do not blend; today we call them genes.

blocks.h: Heredity isn’t like mixing red and white paint into pink; it’s like a deck of cards. Each card stays as it is; the deck is simply reshuffled and dealt again each time. A card that was face down (a recessive trait) may still turn up in the next round.

Mendel read his paper to the Natural Science Society in Brno in February and March 1865, and it was published in 1866. At the time hardly anyone saw its importance. Only in 1900 was it rediscovered by several scientists, and Mendel came to be honored as the father of genetics.

In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of the monastery; from then on his administrative duties were heavy and his research dwindled. His use of statistics and mathematics to tackle biological questions was very advanced for its time.

In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher argued that Mendel’s data were “too good to be true” and suspected they had been adjusted. The debate went on for decades; a 2008 book by several scholars reviewed the analyses, and most concluded there is no evidence that Mendel deliberately falsified anything, though explanations still differ for why the data came so close to expectation.
Mendel’s pea paper was read in 1865 and published in 1866 in volume 4 of the proceedings of the Natural Science Society in Brno.
Mendel was an Augustinian friar and Catholic priest who later became abbot of the Abbey of St Thomas.
Fisher held that Mendel’s data were too close to the theoretical values; the controversy is not fully settled, but most scholars do not believe it was deliberate fraud.

Part of Mendel’s reason for entering the monastery was to receive a free education and be spared financial worries; there is little historical evidence on how his faith related to his motives for research, so it should not be overdramatized.
That life is passed from generation to generation by a stable, predictable set of laws reflects the Creator’s order and faithfulness. This is a philosophical inference.
His wisdom: great laws revealed in small things
Mendel’s discovery came from the most ordinary of places: a monastery garden, one pea after another. God often reveals His great wisdom in small things.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
Mendel went unrecognized in his lifetime, yet his work bore fruit more than thirty years later. In God’s eyes, faithful work is never wasted.

He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field, which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”
Notice the ways you resemble your parents, and the ways you are uniquely you. Every one of you is God’s carefully crafted work.
Reflect: Have I become discouraged because my efforts go unseen? Am I willing to hand the results over to the God who gives the increase?
Prayer: God who makes all things grow, thank You for showing Your wisdom in ordinary things. Help me to be faithful where no one sees, and to leave the results in Your hands. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: From the temporary to the eternal: Mendel was not recognized in his lifetime, but faithful work in God’s hands never comes to nothing.
Repetition: he counted peas day after day. Change in our lives also takes repeated practice; it doesn’t happen all at once.
Give thanks in everything: give the credit for the results to God who gives the increase, not to yourself.

blocks.h: This week: Choose one small thing you are doing that no one sees. Do it faithfully every day this week, and offer it to God in prayer.
Quiz

quiz.q: What plant did Mendel use for his heredity experiments?
quiz.e: Peas have clear contrasting traits, and their pollination is easy to control.

quiz.q: After crossing pure-bred round and wrinkled peas, what was the approximate ratio of round to wrinkled in the second generation?
quiz.e: The recessive wrinkled trait reappeared in the second generation, making up about a quarter.

quiz.q: When was Mendel’s paper rediscovered?
quiz.e: More than thirty years after publication, the scientific world finally took notice.

units.title: The Dialogue Between Science and Faith
units.sub: Science and faith are not eternal enemies, but friends who can have an honest conversation.

share.v: For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.

blocks.h: One of the pioneers of the idea that “the universe had a beginning” was a Catholic priest. In 1927 the Belgian Georges Lemaître (1894–1966) proposed that the universe is expanding, and in 1931 that it began from a “primeval atom,” the forerunner of the Big Bang theory.
In a 1933 interview with The New York Times, he said: “There were two ways of arriving at the truth. I decided to follow them both.”

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
Where did the “conflict thesis” come from?

The impression that “science and religion are always at war” comes largely from two books of the late nineteenth century: Draper’s History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and White’s A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom (1896).

Most historians of science today believe these two books had an obvious agenda and reduced a complex history to a war. In reality, the relationship has included conflict, but also cooperation, independence and dialogue, varying by era and by person.

Science and faith are like a telescope and a letter. The telescope shows you how tall a distant mountain is; the letter tells you that the writer loves you. Read the letter with a telescope, or measure the mountain with the letter, and you’ll get it wrong; but together they can help you know the same friend.

Lemaître himself was careful not to mix scientific theory with theology. When Pope Pius XII gave an address in 1951 that seemed to equate the beginning of the universe directly with the biblical creation, Lemaître was uneasy: scientific theories may be revised, and faith should not be tied to any one scientific model.

The American geneticist Francis Collins led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the U.S. National Institutes of Health. At 27 he read C. S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity and came to faith; in 2006 he published The Language of God, and in 2007 he founded BioLogos, devoted to dialogue between science and faith.

In 2009 the Pew Research Center surveyed scientists of the American Association for the Advancement of Science: about 33% believed in God, 18% in a universal spirit or higher power, and 41% in neither. The sociologist Elaine Howard Ecklund’s research has also found that religious belief among scientists is more diverse than commonly assumed.

items.h: Science and religion are inherently opposed; when one advances, the other retreats. Most historians of science consider this inconsistent with the full historical picture.
Science asks “how does it work?” while faith asks “why, and what does it mean?” Each has its own domain, and they do not interfere with each other.
The two overlap and can question and enrich each other; for example, the order and origin of the universe raise deep philosophical and theological questions.

blocks.h: Lemaître was a Catholic priest who proposed an expanding universe in 1927 and, in 1931 in the journal Nature, proposed that the universe began from a “primeval atom.”
The conflict thesis, that “science and religion have always been at war,” is largely a nineteenth-century construction; most historians of science consider it an oversimplification of history.
According to the 2009 Pew survey, about 51% of scientists in the American Association for the Advancement of Science believed in God or some higher power, lower than the general American public.
Science describes how creation works, but cannot by itself answer “why does anything exist?” The order of creation points to a Creator; this is a philosophical inference.
His faithfulness and righteousness: truth has only one source
Having walked through this hall, we see one thing: God is the source of all truth. Whether in the laboratory or in the Bible, whatever is true comes from Him.
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.
Science lets us see God’s works, but it cannot replace God’s Word. The fear of God is the true starting point of all knowledge.
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.

Think back over the people in this hall: Kepler, Galileo, Newton, Pascal, Boyle, Faraday, Maxwell, Mendel, Lemaître. Each had strengths and weaknesses, but all of them searched for truth within creation.
Reflect: Have I ever avoided questions because I was afraid of science, or looked down on faith because I worshiped science?

Prayer: Lord of all truth, thank You for letting all created things declare Your glory. Help me to fear You and love the truth, and in the dialogue between science and faith, to bear witness to You with gentleness and humility. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: scientific discoveries can enrich our understanding of the world, but the direction of our lives is set by the Bible.
People matter more than issues: when talking with people who see things differently, care about the person first, then discuss the ideas; don’t mock and don’t belittle.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: whether scientists or ordinary people, all discoveries belong to the Lord who made all things.

blocks.h: This week: find a friend who has questions about faith, buy them a cup of coffee, ask one sincere question, and listen patiently without rushing to argue.

Congratulations on completing the History of Science Hall! From the birth of modern science to Kepler’s orbits, Newton’s laws, Faraday and Maxwell’s light, Mendel’s peas and today’s dialogue, you have seen a faithful, wise and righteous God who keeps inviting people to explore His works.
Quiz

quiz.q: Who was Lemaître, a pioneer of the idea that “the universe had a beginning”?
quiz.e: In 1927 and 1931 he proposed the expanding universe and the “primeval atom.”

quiz.q: The conflict thesis, that “science and religion have always been at war,” became popular mainly through books from which era?
quiz.e: The books by Draper (1874) and White (1896) were very influential.

quiz.q: According to Proverbs 1:7, what is the beginning of knowledge?
quiz.e: “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge.”

units.title: Pasteur and Lister: The Invisible Enemy
units.sub: A pair of unwashed hands and a flask with a bent neck rewrote humanity’s statistics of life and death.

share.v: Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

blocks.h: On August 13, 1865, a 47-year-old Hungarian doctor died in an asylum on the outskirts of Vienna, of sepsis from an infected wound. His name was Semmelweis, and all his life he had begged his colleagues to do one thing: wash their hands.

In that very same year, a surgeon in Glasgow, Scotland, used carbolic acid in an operation for the first time. One man fell, and another carried on, and their work went on to save countless mothers and children.

But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
Semmelweis: the death rate hidden in the hands

In the 1840s the Vienna General Hospital had two maternity wards. In the section run by doctors and medical students, the death rate among mothers was about three times that of the section run by midwives. In 1847 a colleague of his was cut by a scalpel during an autopsy and soon died, with symptoms very similar to childbed fever. Semmelweis reasoned that doctors were carrying something deadly from the dissecting room to the delivery room.
He required hand washing with a chlorinated lime solution before entering the maternity ward. The death rate in the First Clinic fell from 18.3% in April 1847 to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July.

Imagine you are a doctor who gives everything you have, busy in the delivery room until late at night. Someone walks up with a table of statistics and says: what is killing these mothers may be your hands. This is exactly what many doctors heard back then. No wonder it was so hard to accept.

Most of his colleagues rejected him. In 1849 he was dismissed from the Vienna General Hospital, in 1861 he published a book, and later he wrote open letters accusing his colleagues in increasingly harsh language. His data were right, but at that time there was no germ theory to explain why.
Pasteur: the flask with the bent neck

Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) was a chemist, not a physician. The dispute of the day was whether life could arise on its own when broth spoils. He drew out the neck of a flask into a curved swan neck, so that air could get in but dust was caught in the bend. After the broth was boiled, it stayed clear; but if the flask was tilted so the broth touched the dust in the neck, microbes soon grew. In 1862 he received a prize from the French Academy of Sciences for this.
Lister: bringing the principle of fermentation into the operating room

Joseph Lister (1827–1912) read Pasteur’s work and reasoned that the festering of wounds is also caused by tiny living things in the air. In 1865 he began treating wounds with carbolic acid, and in 1867 he published in The Lancet. By his own statistics, deaths after amputation fell from 16 deaths in 35 cases (about 45%) to 6 deaths in 40 cases (about 15%).
Rabies: a nine-year-old boy

On July 6, 1885, nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten more than a dozen times by a rabid dog, was brought to Paris on the third day. Pasteur had no license to practice medicine, so the physician Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave the vaccine, not yet tested on humans, in a dozen or so injections over about ten days. The boy lived. In 1888 the Pasteur Institute was founded.

At Pasteur’s seventieth birthday celebration in 1892, Lister came in person to honor him, and a painter recorded the scene. The two men came from different countries and different church traditions, yet they struggled against the same enemy.
The historians’ other side

Pasteur’s laboratory notebooks were not made public until the 1970s. In 1995 the historian Gerald Geison pointed out that Pasteur publicly said the vaccine had been tried on 50 dogs, while the notebooks show only about 11; that before treating Meister he had already tried it on two patients, one of whom died; and that he also concealed some of the methods behind the anthrax vaccine. Heroic biographies often skip over these things. Lister’s numbers were likewise questioned by his contemporaries: the sample was small and he used past cases as the comparison. He himself admitted the numbers were few. History later proved the direction right, but the process was not as clean as in a storybook.
First let’s separate what is certain, what is under discussion and what is inference.
After Semmelweis introduced chlorinated lime hand washing in 1847, the death rate in the Vienna First Obstetric Clinic fell sharply; during his lifetime most of his colleagues did not accept it.
Pasteur used experiment to refute the then-current theory of spontaneous generation, and the Meister case in 1885 was the first known successful treatment with a rabies vaccine.

Lister’s statistics show amputation mortality falling from about 45% to 15%. Later generations affirmed the direction, but his numbers had a small sample and a loosely controlled comparison group, and were disputed at the time.

Vaccines are still saving lives today: a 2024 modeling study estimated that global immunization programs averted about 154 million deaths over 50 years. This is a model estimate, not a count case by case.
These scientists’ compassion for patients echoes the Bible’s regard for people. This is a faith interpretation; it does not mean that bacteriology proved Christianity.
What did Pasteur believe?

Many sayings about faith are attributed to Pasteur online, and this unit uses none of them. The most famous, about “the faith of a Breton peasant woman,” is regarded as spurious even by two of his descendants; the story of him saying the rosary on a train to rebuke university students also has no reliable source. The biography by his son-in-law describes his absolute confidence in God and eternity; his grandson, however, said he kept only a kind of spirituality without religious practice.

items.h: Based on his son-in-law’s biography and testimony from Catholic circles, he had faith all his life and at the end turned to the church of his ancestors.
Based on his grandson’s account, he believed in something transcendent but seldom practiced religion, and he objected to mixing science and religion.
He was not an atheist, but the sources disagree about how deep his specific faith ran. We do not need to put one more word in his mouth.

blocks.h: The record on Lister is simpler: he was born into a Quaker family, and in 1856 he married Agnes, who was not a Quaker, and so left the Society of Friends and joined the Scottish Episcopal Church. A Christian website quotes him as saying he believed the fundamental teachings of Christianity, but it gives no original source, so we treat it only as supporting evidence.

Some also say the Law of Moses already taught bacteriology. The purity regulations may indeed have had hygienic effects, but the text speaks of holiness, not of microbes. The hand-washing dispute in Jesus’ day was likewise a question of tradition and ritual (Mark 7:3). Letting the text say what it means to say wins the trust of friends better than forcing science onto it.
Goodness sees the smallest person

Nineteenth-century mothers were mostly poor, and often came to the public hospital to give birth because they could not afford anything else. For the sake of a group of women whose names no one remembers, one doctor sacrificed his career. Where does this compassion for strangers come from? Jesus answered that question with a story, and then told us to do likewise.
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

To be clear: germs and disease are not the same as sin, and those who fall ill are certainly not being punished. But there is one similarity: the deadliest things are often invisible, and people are least willing to admit that they are on their own hands. Semmelweis told doctors “the problem is on your hands”; the Bible tells everyone the problem is in our hearts. Jesus did not merely hand us a basin of water; He Himself bore our sins.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.
The next time you wash your hands, wash slowly for twenty seconds. Think of the mothers who lived because of this small act, and think of who paid the price for your heart.
Reflect: What “invisible thing” is in my heart, such that when others kindly point it out, my first reaction is anger?

Pray: Merciful Lord, thank You for seeing our wounds, and thank You for saving countless people through so many doctors and nurses. Take away my pride, and make me willing to hear the truth; let Your precious blood wash away all my sin, so that I too can show compassion to the wounded around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: When someone points out my blind spot, first say “please tell me more,” and only then defend myself.
Jesus is my example: When He saw the wounded, He was moved with compassion. I too will stop and see the one who is being overlooked around me.
People matter more than tasks: Every number on a table of statistics is a person. At work, remember the other person’s name and situation first.

blocks.h: This week: Write a thank-you card (or send a message) to a medical worker, caregiver or cleaner, thanking them specifically for one small thing they do. If you have a physical complaint that persists, please see a doctor.
Pass it on: Have you ever had someone tell you a truth you did not want to hear, and later found out they were right?
Quiz

quiz.q: What did Semmelweis use to greatly reduce the death rate of mothers?
o: Requiring doctors to wash their hands with a chlorinated lime solution
Having mothers give birth at home instead
quiz.e: In 1847 he required hand washing with a chlorinated lime solution before entering the maternity ward, and the death rate in the First Clinic dropped sharply.

quiz.q: How does this unit treat the saying “the faith of a Breton peasant woman,” attributed to Pasteur?
o: It was written in Pasteur’s own hand late in life
It comes from his Nobel Prize speech
His descendants regarded it as spurious, so it is not used
quiz.e: Pasteur never won a Nobel Prize (the prize did not yet exist when he died), and his descendants regarded the saying as spurious. Testimony must be built on facts that can be checked.

quiz.q: After telling the parable of the Good Samaritan, what did Jesus say to the lawyer?
o: Go and study who your neighbor is
quiz.e: Luke 10:37. Jesus turned “who is my neighbor?” into “whose neighbor will I be?”

units.title: Carver: The Slave’s Son and the Peanut
units.sub: He did not invent peanut butter. What he did was more worth remembering than that legend, and harder.

share.v: For his God instructs him in right judgment and teaches him.

blocks.h: While he was still an infant, he and his mother were carried off by night raiders. Later someone found him and brought him back, but his mother was never heard of again. He could not even say for certain what year he was born.

That child later stood before the United States Congress to testify, and after his death was given the first national monument in America to honor an African American. His grave marker reads that he could have added fortune to fame, but caring for neither, he found happiness and honor in being helpful to the world. His name was George Washington Carver.
For his God instructs him in right judgment and teaches him.
First, debunking a legend

You have probably heard that Carver invented peanut butter, and also invented 300 uses for the peanut. The first claim is wrong. Peanut butter is not even on the list of his peanut products compiled by later generations.

The second needs care. Carver himself said in 1937 that there were more than three hundred, but he left no list; after his death the museum listed 287 items, many of which were not original to him and some of which nearly duplicate one another. The National Park Service web page still says “325 kinds” today, which shows how hard the number is to pin down.

A legend is like a poster on a neighborhood bulletin board that keeps getting a new one pasted over it. Everyone thinks they are posting good news: peanut dealers want advertising, schools want donations, writers want a hero, the Black community wants a role model. Only when you peel down to the bottom layer do you see a real person.
From a kidnapped infant to Tuskegee

Carver was born around 1864 or 1865 in Missouri, enslaved by Moses and Susan Carver. After he was recovered, the couple raised him. In his teens he left home to look for schooling, supporting himself by doing laundry and housework for others, and drifted about Missouri and Kansas for roughly ten years.

In 1896 he earned his master’s degree at Iowa State Agricultural College and became the first Black faculty member there. In October of that year, at the invitation of Booker T. Washington, he went to Tuskegee Institute in Alabama to head its agriculture program. That same year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled racial segregation legal in Plessy.
His real work: saving the soil, saving the tenant farmers

The land around Tuskegee had been drained by cotton and the tenant-farming system. Black tenant farmers were in debt and short of food, and the land grew poorer with every planting. Carver taught them ways to farm without buying chemical fertilizer, rotating crops such as peanuts, cowpeas and sweet potatoes. His peanut research was part of this fight from the beginning, both enriching the soil and giving poor people who owned no land a source of protein.

The formal writings he left behind are mainly practical pamphlets for farmers, and the most popular was the 1916 How to Grow the Peanut and 105 Ways of Preparing It for Human Consumption. He also designed a movable school, using a wagon to bring agricultural education directly to farmers’ doorsteps.

Most scientists write up their results for their peers; Carver wrote his for people who could not even afford fertilizer. The real nameplate on his laboratory was nailed up in a tenant farmer’s kitchen.
Faith, without disguise

Carver joined the Presbyterian church as a young man. From 1907 he led a Bible class on the Tuskegee campus, starting with Genesis 1 and continuing for about thirty years. When he testified before the House Ways and Means Committee in 1921, he cited the words in Genesis 1 in which God gives seed-bearing herbs.

In 1924 he spoke at a church in New York and said that he kept no books in his laboratory and worked by God’s inspiration. The New York Times promptly published an editorial, “Scientists Don’t Talk That Way,” criticizing him. The criticism had its point: science needs methods and records that can be checked, and the formulas he left behind were indeed too few. In private letters he responded that what some people were attacking was faith in Christ.
The historians’ verdict

In 1977 the National Park Service historian Barry Mackintosh pointed out that almost none of the new uses Carver found for peanuts and sweet potatoes was adopted by industry on a large scale, and that the biggest growth in peanut production came before he became famous. The legend was made mainly by reporters and peanut interests, and Carver’s role was one of passive complicity more than active deception. Mackintosh also concluded that what kind of man Carver was matters more than what he did.

Mark Hersey’s 2011 environmental biography shifts the focus back to the land and calls him a prophet of sustainable agriculture, while admitting that he never truly challenged the tenant system or the racial hierarchy of the South.
The person with the most legends needs to be checked layer by layer.
Carver was born into slavery and recovered after being kidnapped as an infant; he went to Tuskegee in 1896 after earning his master’s degree, and died on January 5, 1943.
Carver did not invent peanut butter, and it is not on his list of peanut products.
The “300 uses for the peanut” comes from Carver’s own statement, and there is no complete list to check; of the 287 items compiled after his death, many were not original.

His real contribution to agriculture lay mainly in education and in extending soil-building methods to poor farmers, not in industrial invention. This is the mainstream view of contemporary historians, though details are still debated.

Popular accounts say Edison once tried to hire him at a large salary. The scholarly sources we consulted show no reliable documentation, so this unit does not use it; his friendship with Ford, however, did exist.

Carver’s faith was inseparable from his drive to serve the poor. This shows that faith can nurture a certain use of science, but it does not mean his research methods were therefore more reliable, and it does not prove the Christian faith true.
Perspectives Room
How should we regard a Christian who has been turned into a myth?

items.h: Carver’s fame was mainly a product of what society needed: white people used him to prove that the racial system could have successful Black men, and businesses used him to sell peanuts. His scientific contribution is badly overestimated, and tolerating the exaggeration was also a fault of his.

The system he lived in gave Black scientists very few resources or channels for publication. He chose to spend his strength on the poorest people, and the cost was that he left little academic output. Tolerating the exaggeration was a fault, but it does not cancel that choice.

blocks.h: He teaches the one who farms
Isaiah uses a farmer as a parable: plowing and sowing each have their season, and barley and wheat each have their place. The prophet says that even this common sense is taught by God.

Does he who plows to sow plow continually? Does he keep turning the soil and breaking the clods? When he has leveled its surface, doesn’t he plant the dill, and scatter the cumin seed, and put in the wheat in rows, the barley in the appointed place, and the spelt in its place? For his God instructs him in right judgment and teaches him.
The Bible also asks the land to rest, so that people do not squeeze the soil to its last drop. Seeing the Creator’s gifts in the ground was the instinct of Carver’s whole life.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation nor turning shadow.

His grave marker says he cared for neither fortune nor fame, and put being helpful to the world first. The source of that heart lies in a greater Servant. Christ, who was in the form of God, took the form of a servant and died on a cross. Humankind used slavery to treat people as goods, but the Son of God Himself went into the lowest place, and rose from the dead, and gave dignity back to everyone who has been trampled.

Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.

Pick up a peanut or a handful of rice and look at it for ten seconds. Think of the soil behind this mouthful, the farmers, the unseen root nodules and microbes. Then give thanks for the hands that grew it.
Reflect: For whom is my expertise written? Is there someone who cannot afford it, cannot understand it, or is ignored by everyone, for whom I could go a little further?

Pray: Father of lights, every good gift comes from You. Thank You for seeing the kidnapped infant, and for seeing the nameless tenant farmer in the field. Lord Jesus, You took the form of a servant, and died and rose for me. Take away my love of being praised, and let me use what I have learned to serve the least of my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Jesus is my example: He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant. My gifts can also flow downward: ask first who needs them most, and only then who will applaud.
Let Jesus receive all the glory: When others exaggerate about me, I should correct them myself. Carver’s fault reminds us that silent consent is also a choice.
Change your mindset, change your life: Turn from “how much can my profession earn?” to “whom can my profession help?” and the same job begins to look different.

blocks.h: This week: Translate one of your skills into words your neighbor can understand. Teaching an older person to recognize scam messages, helping a new immigrant read a form, or teaching a child to grow a pot of beans all count.
Pass it on: If someone wrote your epitaph one day, would you want it to say how much you earned, or whom you helped?
Quiz

quiz.q: Which statement about Carver and peanut butter is correct?
o: He invented peanut butter and patented it
He did not invent peanut butter, and it is not even on his product list
He sold peanut butter to Ford
quiz.e: This is the most widespread misconception. Peanut butter already existed before he became famous.

quiz.q: What do historians regard as Carver’s most substantial contribution?
o: Agricultural education that helped poor tenant farmers restore their soil and improve their lives
Inventing hundreds of best-selling industrial products
Abolishing the tenant-farming system in the South
quiz.e: His main work was in education and extension; Hersey also points out that he never truly challenged the tenant system.

quiz.q: What did The New York Times criticize Carver for in 1924?
o: He credited scientific discoveries to God’s inspiration, which is not how a scientist talks
quiz.e: The editorial was titled “Scientists Don’t Talk That Way.” Faith was his motivation, but science still depends on methods and records that can be checked.

units.title: Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi
units.sub: The Chinese word for “geometry” in your textbook came from a translation ground out character by character, in Beijing, by an Italian priest and a Shanghai scholar-official.

share.v: Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.

blocks.h: The Chinese words you drew in middle school, “parallel lines” and “right angle,” can in many cases be traced back to Beijing in 1607. An Italian priest dictated, and a Shanghai scholar-official took up the brush, to put the mathematics of the ancient Greek Euclid into Chinese.
At that time Chinese had no ready-made words for it. They walked and paved the road at the same time.
Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.
A priest in Confucian dress

Matteo Ricci (1552–1610) was an Italian Jesuit who studied in Rome under the mathematician Christoph Clavius. He reached Macau in 1582 and entered mainland China the following year. At first he wore the robes of a Buddhist monk; later he found that the scholar-officials were the real learned class of Chinese society, so he changed to Confucian dress, and in 1601 he entered Beijing.

He could recite the classics from memory, draw a map of the world and calculate an eclipse, and he also wrote The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu shiyi), speaking of God in the language of the Chinese classics. After his death the Wanli Emperor allowed him to be buried in Beijing, a rare exception at that time.
The jinshi Xu Guangqi

Xu Guangqi (1562–1633) was from Shanghai. He met Ricci in Nanjing in 1600, was baptized in 1603 with the Christian name Paul, and passed the jinshi examination the following year. He later rose to Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of the Cabinet, and also wrote the Complete Treatise on Agriculture (Nongzheng quanshu), promoting the planting of sweet potatoes, out of concern for whether common people could survive a famine.
1607: six books of the Elements

Working from Clavius’s Latin edition with commentary, the two translated the first 6 books of Euclid’s Elements, published in 1607. Xu wanted to finish all fifteen books, but Ricci advised stopping for the time being. The remaining nine books were completed only in 1857 by Li Shanlan and the Protestant missionary Alexander Wylie, 250 years later.

Translating this book was like building a bridge between two shores with no map, naming every plank as you laid it. Ricci passed the pieces over from the western bank, and Xu Guangqi caught them on the eastern bank and asked: this word, will Chinese readers understand it?

China already had a deep mathematical tradition; the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art and Liu Hui’s commentary are proof. What the Elements brought that was new was a way of arguing that builds a whole edifice step by step from a few axioms. Xu Guangqi valued this greatly: he thought the book could train people to think rigorously.
The Chongzhen Calendar Treatise

The Ming calendar repeatedly failed to predict eclipses accurately. In 1629 Xu Guangqi was ordered to lead the calendar reform, and he invited Jesuits such as Johann Schreck, Giacomo Rho and Adam Schall. He died in 1633, and the monumental Chongzhen Calendar Treatise was completed afterward. The Ming fell before it could be promulgated, and Schall adapted it and presented it to the Qing, where it became the basis of the calendar from then on.

Here is a limitation that must be stated honestly: this treatise was based mainly on the system of Tycho Brahe and did not adopt Copernicus’s sun-centered theory as its framework. Rome had already banned Copernicus’s book in 1616, and the missionaries worked under that constraint. The science that came over was real, but not complete.
Mission and science: be clear about motives

Ricci made clear in his letters that his science was meant to open the way for mission. There is no need to hide this. Xu Guangqi’s motive was practical learning to save the country, and also faith. Scholars such as Jacques Gernet go further and question whether what the scholar-officials accepted was really Christianity, or a Confucianized moral teaching. This question has not been settled to this day.
Let’s separate fact from interpretation.
In 1607 the first six books of the Elements, translated jointly by Ricci and Xu Guangqi, were published; the last nine books were completed by Li Shanlan and Alexander Wylie in 1857.
Xu Guangqi was baptized in 1603 and headed the calendar reform of the Chongzhen era.
In 1715 Pope Clement XI issued Ex illa die forbidding the Chinese rites, and in 1721 the Kangxi Emperor ordered a ban on the faith; only in 1939 did the Holy See relax the ban with Plane Compertum.
A good number of modern Chinese mathematical terms originate in this translation. Exactly which words, scholars’ research still debates in detail.
How much of the faith of scholar-officials like Xu Guangqi was Christian and how much was Confucianized moral teaching is still disputed in scholarship.
A person can love truth, country and Christ wholeheartedly all at once, and these three do not necessarily conflict. This is a faith interpretation, and cannot be proved by a historical case.
Perspectives Room
The Rites Controversy: are offerings to ancestors and to Confucius idol worship?

items.h: Offerings to ancestors and Confucius are social rites expressing filial devotion and respect for teachers, and may be permitted; using “Shangdi” and “Tian” from the Chinese classics to translate God lets the gospel truly enter Chinese culture.

items.n: The strict path of the Dominicans and others
items.h: The rites do contain elements of petitioning the dead and making offerings, and compromise would confuse the faith; the gospel cannot cut back the first commandment in order to be accepted.

items.n: A common Chinese Protestant position today
items.h: Remembrance and filial respect should be kept, but without kneeling or burning incense to pray for blessing; specific practices differ among churches. Most pastors remind us: be respectful in attitude, repair relationships first, and do not use faith to shame our elders.

blocks.h: Truth is not afraid of translation
In Athens Paul did not ask people to learn the Jews’ language first. He began from their altar, and then preached Jesus and the resurrection.

Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you.
The greatest translation in the world was done by God Himself. The eternal Word entered one language, one people, one body that could grow tired.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

But there is one place in translation where nothing can be omitted. Critics often point out that early missionary writings spoke much of the Lord of Heaven and morality and little of the cross, because a crucified king is hard for scholar-officials to respect. Paul met the same difficulty long ago, and he did not revise his manuscript. In every age we must ask ourselves: when I translate the gospel in a friendly way, have I lost the cross and the resurrection in translation?
but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks,

Take a sheet of paper, draw two parallel lines and write the three characters for “parallel lines.” More than four hundred years ago someone racked his brain over this word. Thank God for everyone who has translated truth for us, including those who translated the Bible into your mother tongue.
Reflect: In front of my relatives and colleagues, have I put my faith into words they can understand? Have I skipped past Jesus’ cross in order to be liked?

Pray: Lord who became flesh, You came among us in person and spoke words we could understand. Thank You for going to the cross for me and rising from the dead. Give me Xu Guangqi’s earnestness and Ricci’s patience, so that I may honor culture without discounting Your gospel. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: People matter more than tasks: Ricci first learned the language and made friends, and only then spoke of faith. Sharing the gospel begins with respecting the other person, not with winning the argument.

The Bible is my standard: When dealing with cultural questions such as ancestor rites, we neither reject culture across the board nor let culture rewrite the gospel; we return to the Bible to discern.

Life first, then relationship, then ministry: Xu Guangqi’s faith flowed into his calendar reform and his agricultural treatise. Faith does not stay only on Sundays; it is also in the fruit of your work.

blocks.h: This week: Ask an unbelieving elder or friend: what matters most to your family at Qingming or the New Year, and why? Only listen; do not argue.
Pass it on: Do you think a person can do serious scholarship, love their own culture, and believe in God at the same time? Do you know anyone like that?
Quiz

quiz.q: How many books of the Elements did Ricci and Xu Guangqi translate in 1607?
quiz.e: The last nine books had to wait until 1857, when Li Shanlan and Alexander Wylie completed them.

quiz.q: What limitation did the astronomy that came with the Chongzhen Calendar Treatise have?
o: It was based mainly on Tycho’s system, not on Copernicus’s sun-centered theory as its framework
It had no mathematics at all
It was only applicable in Rome
quiz.e: The science was real, but what came over was not complete.

quiz.q: What was the core question of the Rites Controversy?
o: Whether missionaries could wear Confucian dress
Whether offerings to ancestors and Confucius are social rites or religious worship
quiz.e: The Jesuits and the Dominicans and others held different views. In 1715 Rome forbade the rites, and in 1721 the Kangxi Emperor ordered a ban on the faith.

units.title: Believing Scientists Today
units.sub: There are Nobel laureates who believe in Christ, and many more top scientists who do not. Both things are true. How should we think about that?

share.v: Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

blocks.h: He led the Human Genome Project and finished reading the genetic code of humankind. In his youth he was an atheist; it was while in medical school, stopped by a patient’s question, that he began to investigate seriously.

His name is Francis Collins. Before you hurry to forward this: in the corridor of the same laboratory there are colleagues just as brilliant as he is who do not believe in God. That is what this unit is about.
Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.
A few believing scientists of today

items: Francis Collins: A geneticist who directed the U.S. National Human Genome Research Institute from 1993 to 2008 and served as Director of the National Institutes of Health from 2009 to 2021. Originally an atheist, he came to faith, wrote The Language of God (2006), and founded BioLogos.

William Phillips: A physicist at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology who shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics with Steven Chu and Claude Cohen-Tannoudji for laser cooling of atoms. He openly says he is a Christian and takes part in church life.

Rosalind Picard: A professor at the MIT Media Lab and a pioneer of the field of “affective computing.” She says she was once a staunch atheist, and that after meeting thoughtful, intelligent believers she re-examined the evidence and began to take faith seriously.

Jennifer Wiseman: An astrophysicist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center who has worked on the Hubble Space Telescope project and also directed the American Association for the Advancement of Science’s program of dialogue on science and religion.

John Polkinghorne (1930–2021): Professor of mathematical physics at Cambridge and a Fellow of the Royal Society who, in mid-career, resigned his chair and became an Anglican priest; he received the Templeton Prize in 2002.

Don Page: A theoretical physicist at the University of Alberta in Canada who worked with Stephen Hawking on black holes and is an evangelical Christian. The two differed on God, yet their friendship lasted many years.

blocks.h: A list is like a group photo. A group photo can tell you “these people once stood together,” but it cannot tell you “everyone standing together is right.” Outside the frame stands a large crowd of equally distinguished colleagues who do not believe in God.
What the surveys say

In 2009 the Pew Research Center surveyed members of the American Association for the Advancement of Science: about 33% believed in God, about 18% believed in some universal spirit or higher power, and about 41% believed in neither; in a 2006 Pew survey of the general American public, about 83% believed in God.

The sociologist Elaine Howard Ecklund, in her 2010 Science vs. Religion, surveyed nearly 1,700 scientists at top American research universities: about a third were atheists and about 30% were agnostics. Among top scientists, the proportion who do not believe is clearly higher than in the general public.

She also found another side: many scientists who do not believe still have spiritual pursuits, and some are unimpressed by the public image of a conflict between science and faith. She thinks that scientists’ unbelief may owe as much to their upbringing as to their scientific training. Scholars are still discussing this point, and the situation differs from country to country.
What this list is for

Citing famous people to support faith is, in logic, called an appeal to authority. A Nobel laureate in physics is an authority on laser cooling, but on whether Jesus rose from the dead he is simply a serious reader. The same goes for atheists who cite Hawking. This list can do only one thing: refute the claim that “people with a scientific mind cannot believe in God.” One counterexample is enough; asking it to do more goes beyond what it can do.
This topic is the easiest one to pad, so let’s mark each claim separately.
Collins, Phillips, Picard, Wiseman, Polkinghorne and Page are all scientists recognized in their professions, and all openly profess the Christian faith.
The proportion of American scientists who believe in God is clearly lower than in the general public.

Scientific training itself has not been shown to cause unbelief; upbringing may matter just as much. This is Ecklund’s interpretation; the scholarly community is still discussing it, and it varies by country.
Trends over time in the proportion of religious belief among scientists differ with the definitions and samples used, so comparisons must be made with care.
“The existence of believing scientists” shows that science and faith need not conflict. It does not prove that faith is true; likewise, unbelieving scientists do not prove that faith is false.
Perspectives Room
What does it mean that top scientists are less likely to believe in God?

items.h: The better people become at thinking with evidence, the less they need supernatural explanations. The correlation speaks for itself, and believing scientists are a minority of exceptions who keep their faith and their work in different rooms.

The elite academic world has its own culture and selection effects, and correlation is not causation. For many researchers faith was formed before their training, and unbelief may also come from family background. The question itself must in the end be decided by evidence and argument, not by headcount.

blocks.h: What really needs checking is not a list
The Bible never asks anyone to believe because famous people believe. The psalmist encourages people to go and investigate for themselves.
Yahweh’s works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them.
Paul too did not build faith on a list. He brought everyone straight to one thing: Christ died, was buried, was raised, and was seen. This is the place where the whole faith stands or falls.

For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.

So whether one is clever or not, the road to God is the same for everyone. Paul said long ago that among those called, not many are wise. God’s grace sets no IQ threshold, and does not give a little more of a discount to anyone because they have won a prize.

For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong.
Think of an unbelieving friend you know and respect. Do not treat him as a problem to be solved. Thank God for his earnestness and goodness, and pray for him once.
Reflect: Do I believe in Jesus because I have investigated for myself, or because people I admire believe? If a famous Christian I look up to were to fall, would my faith still stand?

Pray: Lord Jesus, You are the truth. Save me from a faith that gets its courage from famous names, and let me stand on Your cross and resurrection. Thank You for not abandoning me because I know so little. Give me humility, that I may respect my unbelieving friends and gently explain why I have hope. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Letting God be God and people be people: Even the most outstanding Christian is only a human being. Give the glory to the Lord Jesus, and do not hang your faith on someone else.
The Bible is my standard: Other people’s testimonies can open a door, but the investigating you must do yourself. Read the Gospels and face for yourself who Jesus is.
People matter more than tasks: Do not treat unbelieving friends as opponents in a debate. Respect their earnestness; the relationship matters more than winning.

blocks.h: This week: Delete one “famous person comes to faith” message that you forwarded but are actually unsure of; if you have forwarded something known to be wrong, correct it with the person you sent it to.
Pass it on: Do you think science and faith must conflict? How did you form that view?
Quiz

quiz.q: What is the “list of believing scientists” best used for?
o: Proving that the Christian faith is true
Refuting the claim that “scientists cannot believe in God”
Showing that most scientists believe in God
quiz.e: One counterexample can refute “impossible,” but it cannot prove that faith is true.

quiz.q: According to Pew’s 2009 survey of American scientists, about what share believe in God?
quiz.e: About 33%, clearly lower than the roughly 83% of the general public (Pew, 2006).

quiz.q: Where does the Bible place the crux of the faith?
o: The number of believers who have won Nobel Prizes
The death and resurrection of Christ
quiz.e: 1 Corinthians 15:3-5. The faith stands or falls on whether this event is true.

questions.q: If the universe is an accident, why is it orderly and understandable to us?
Are science and faith really enemies?
